questions.q: Why does this lesson say launching a new capability to every department simultaneously is almost always the wrong sequencing choice?
options: ServiceNow technically prevents simultaneous rollouts
It multiplies every unknown by the number of departments involved, so a design flaw is discovered everywhere at once with no department yet convinced it works
Simultaneous rollout is always faster and therefore always correct
Pilot departments are only needed when the organization has fewer than three departments
questions.explain: A simultaneous launch means a flawed design, or a rough edge, hits every department at the same time, with no proven track record to build confidence on.

questions.q: What is the right criterion for choosing a pilot department, according to this lesson?
options: Whichever department has the most complex approval chain, to prove the hardest case first
The clearest, most contained use case — not the biggest or most strategically important department
Whichever department has the most political influence
Alphabetical order among the departments requesting the capability
questions.explain: A clean win on a contained use case builds real organizational confidence; starting with the hardest department tends to produce a visible struggle instead.

questions.q: Which of these belongs in the SHARED, platform-wide category rather than department-specific, per this lesson?
options: The base intake form, core data model, workflow engine, and notification framework
Department-unique approval routing rules
A department's own specific reporting fields
A field that exists only because one department's process genuinely differs from the rest
questions.explain: Anything every department needs in essentially the same shape belongs in a shared scoped application maintained once, benefiting from every future fix.

questions.q: What expensive outcome does letting a genuinely shared capability get rebuilt per department recreate?
options: A requirement to adopt Domain Separation
A permanent sys_domain tax on every future script
The same duplicate-customization problem that federated-governance guardrails from Lesson 25 exist to prevent
No real cost at all, since departments differ anyway
questions.explain: Rebuilding a shared need per department is the same drift federated governance's naming, review, and shared-component guardrails are meant to stop.

questions.q: In the real rollout sequence this lesson describes, what happens to friction the pilot department surfaces?
options: The fix is applied only to the pilot department's own extension
Friction is documented but deliberately left unfixed until the final department launches
Fixes go into the shared base, so every later department benefits from that fix immediately
The rollout restarts from scratch with a new pilot department
questions.explain: Because the fix lands in the shared base, every subsequent department inherits it automatically rather than hitting the same friction again.
